newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: HK exchange official sees more Singapore listings.
newsitem.headline: HK exchange official sees more Singapore listings.

text.p: A top Hong Kong stock exchange official said on Thursday he expected more Hong Kong companies to seek primary listings in Singapore ahead of the territory's mid-1997 handover to Chinese rule.
Herbert Hui, deputy chief executive of the exchange, said he was not concerned, however, because this could enhance the international profile of Hong Kong companies.
He said that capital raised through Hong Kong's stock market in the first half of this year had nearly doubled the amount raised for all of 1995.
Hui declined to give figures for the amount raised so far this year but said: "This year has seen a lot of infrastructure companies raising capital from the market."

With a large amount of infrastructural work going on in the region, especially in China, the Hong Kong exchange was keen to capitalise on the fund raising needs of companies engaged in such work, he said.
The total amount raised in 1995 -- a weak year for fundraising -- through the Hong Kong exchange was HK$153 billion (US$19.8 billion) against HK$346 billion in 1994.
Hui told reporters at a Hong Kong-Singapore Business Association luncheon: "I think a lot of the companies that come here are offshoots of parents in Hong Kong. The parents are still listed there...
"We are not facing a situation that people are leaving Hong Kong for another jurisdiction. All they are doing is hedging their positions," he said.
Hui refused to comment on speculation that the Jardine group of companies might try to return to the Hong Kong exchange for a secondary listing.
The Jardines group transferred their primary listing to London from Hong Kong in 1992 following a disagreement with Hong Kong regulators over the takeover code.
Two years later the group cancelled its secondary listing in Hong Kong, leaving Singapore as the main Asian exchange for trading Jardine group stocks.

Hui said the Hong Kong exchange would continue to bring more Chinese companies to the market and also ensure greater transparency in the operations of these firms and that they comply with international accounting standards.

Regarding the exchange's role after 1997, when Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule, Hui said the Hong Kong exchange would need to work out an understanding with the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges on how they would work together.
